title: Proof
body_md:
For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in\mathcal X_k$, summing over its two possible
successors gives
\[
 \sum_{z\in\{-1,+1\}}\frac{1+ax_1z}{2}=1,
\]
so $P^{\mathrm{dr}}_{k,a}$ is a Markov kernel. For
$y=(y_1,\ldots,y_k)$, its only possible predecessors are
$x^{(\sigma)}=(\sigma,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$, $\sigma\in\{-1,+1\}$, and
\[
 \sum_{\sigma\in\{-1,+1\}}P^{\mathrm{dr}}_{k,a}(x^{(\sigma)},y)
 =\sum_{\sigma\in\{-1,+1\}}\frac{1+a\sigma y_k}{2}=1.
\]
Thus $P^{\mathrm{dr}}_{k,a}$ is doubly stochastic and $U_k$ is stationary.
Since $a<1$, each prescribed appended sign has conditional probability at
least $(1-a)/2>0$. Hence any $y$ can be reached from any $x$ in $k$ steps by
successively appending $y_1,\ldots,y_k$, which occurs with probability $[(1-a)/2]^k$, so the chain is irreducible. Finally,
for $\mathbf 1=(1,\ldots,1)$,
\[
 P^{\mathrm{dr}}_{k,a}(\mathbf 1,\mathbf 1)=\frac{1+a}{2}>0,
\]
so the chain is aperiodic. A finite irreducible and aperiodic chain is
uniformly ergodic.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an initial word $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$. After $t\leq k$ transitions,
the register has the form
\[
 (x_{t+1},\ldots,x_k,x_1E_1,\ldots,x_tE_t),
\]
where $E_1,\ldots,E_t$ are independent Rademacher variables of mean $a$.
For $t<k$, its law is therefore supported on
\[
 S_{x,t}:=\{y\in\mathcal X_k:(y_1,\ldots,y_{k-t})
       =(x_{t+1},\ldots,x_k)\}.
\]
The final $t$ coordinates are free, so $|S_{x,t}|=2^t$ and
\[
 (P^{\mathrm{dr}}_{k,a})^t(x,S_{x,t})=1,
 \qquad U_k(S_{x,t})=\frac{2^t}{2^k}=2^{-(k-t)}.
\]
The event characterisation of total variation gives
\[
 \left\|(P^{\mathrm{dr}}_{k,a})^t(x,\cdot)-U_k\right\|_{\operatorname{TV}}
 \geq1-2^{-(k-t)}.
\]
This holds for every $x$, so averaging over $x\sim U_k$ yields the first
inequality in~\eqref{eq:register-preflush}, since
\begin{align*}
    \beta_a(t)&=2^{-k}\sum_{x\in\mathcal X_k}
 \left\|(P^{\mathrm{dr}}_{k,a})^t(x,\cdot)-U_k\right\|_{\operatorname{TV}} \geq2^{-k}\sum_{x\in\mathcal X_k}\{1-2^{-(k-t)}\}
 =1-2^{-(k-t)}.
\end{align*}
Since $t<k$ implies $k-t\geq1$, its right-hand side is at least $1/2$.

For the block identity, index the fresh multipliers by coordinate and block.
After $\mathcal B$ complete blocks, the register is
\[
 (x_1W_1,\ldots,x_kW_k),
 \qquad W_i:=\prod_{r=1}^{\mathcal B}E_{i,r},
\]
where all the $E_{i,r}$ are independent Rademacher variables of mean $a$.
The products defining distinct $W_i$ use non-overlapping collections of these
independent multipliers, and
\[
 \mathbb E W_i=\prod_{r=1}^{\mathcal B}\mathbb E E_{i,r}=a^{\mathcal B}.
\]
Since each $W_i$ is $\{-1,+1\}$-valued, $W_1,\ldots,W_k$ are independent
Rademacher of mean $a^{\mathcal B}$.

Let $T_x(w):=x\odot w$ and let $\mu_{\mathcal B}$ be the law of
$(W_1,\ldots,W_k)$. Since $T_x(T_x(w))=w$, the map $T_x$ is its own inverse
and hence a bijection of $\mathcal X_k$. Therefore, for every
$A\subseteq\mathcal X_k$,
\[
 U_k(T_x^{-1}A)=\frac{|T_x^{-1}A|}{2^k}=\frac{|A|}{2^k}=U_k(A).
\]
Moreover, as $A$ ranges over all subsets of $\mathcal X_k$, so does
$T_x^{-1}A$. The event characterisation of total variation therefore gives
\begin{align*}
    \|\mu_{\mathcal B}\circ T_x^{-1}-U_k\|_{\operatorname{TV}}
 &=\sup_A|\mu_{\mathcal B}(T_x^{-1}A)-U_k(T_x^{-1}A)| =\|\mu_{\mathcal B}-U_k\|_{\operatorname{TV}}.
\end{align*}

Thus we may remove the fixed signs $x_i$. A word with $j$ plus signs then
has probability
\[
 2^{-k}(1+a^{\mathcal B})^j(1-a^{\mathcal B})^{k-j},
\]
and there are $\binom kj$ such words. The resulting distance is independent
of $x$, so its average over $x\sim U_k$ is $\beta_a(\mathcal B k)$. The
finite-space formula for total variation consequently gives
\begin{align*}
 \beta_a(\mathcal B k)
 &=\frac12\sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj
   \left|2^{-k}(1+a^{\mathcal B})^j
   (1-a^{\mathcal B})^{k-j}-2^{-k}\right| =B_k(a^{\mathcal B}),
\end{align*}
which proves~\eqref{eq:register-block-identity}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Use the notation of \Cref{lem:h-equivalence}.  That lemma gives the
binomial upper-tail representation~\eqref{eq:Bk-binomial-tail}.  By
\Cref{lem:binomial-equivalent-derivative}, $B_k$ is locally absolutely
continuous and~\eqref{eq:Bk-derivative} holds almost everywhere.  The goal
is to obtain a uniform lower bound of order $\sqrt{k}$
for \(B_k'(a)\) on a range containing \(B_k^{-1}([0,3/8])\).  Integrating
that derivative bound will then control increments of \(B_k^{-1}\).

We next show that the inverse images of \([0,3/8]\) occur where \(a\) is of
order \(1/\sqrt{k}\).  Take \(C=3\) and set \(a=C/\sqrt{k}\).  Under
\(P_a\),
\[
 \mathbb E_aS=ka,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Var}_a(S)=k(1-a^2).
\]
Cantelli's inequality therefore gives
\begin{align*}
 P_a(S\leq0)
 &=P_a(S-ka\leq-ka) \leq\frac{k(1-a^2)}{k(1-a^2)+k^2a^2} =\frac{1-a^2}{1+(k-1)a^2}.
\end{align*}
Substituting \(a=C/\sqrt{k}\) yields
\[
 P_a(S\leq0)
 \leq
 \frac{1-C^2/k}{1+C^2(1-1/k)}
 <\frac{1}{1+C^2}=\frac1{10}.
\]
Hence \(P_a(S>0)>9/10\), whereas symmetry gives
\(P_0(S>0)\leq1/2\).  Since total variation dominates the difference in
probabilities of any fixed event,
\[
 B_k(C/\sqrt{k})
 \geq P_a(S>0)-P_0(S>0)
 >\frac9{10}-\frac12
 =\frac25>\frac38.
\]
Together with \(B_k(0)=0\), this shows that every generalised inverse of a
level in \([0,3/8]\) lies in \([0,C/\sqrt{k}]\), once \(k>C^2\).  The
argument below will also prove strict increase on this interval, after
which these generalised inverses are ordinary inverses.

It remains to lower-bound the binomial atom in
\eqref{eq:Bk-derivative}.  Fix \(0\leq a\leq C/\sqrt{k}\).  Since
\(r_k(a)\) is the first point in a lattice of spacing two strictly above
\(kh(a)\), write
\[
 r_k(a)=kh(a)+u,
 \qquad 0<u\leq2.
\]
Put
\[
 n=k-1,
 \qquad p=\frac{1+a}{2},
 \qquad j=j_k(a)-1.
\]
For $k>C^2$, the bounds on $h$ give $0\leq h(a)<1$.  Hence
$0<r_k(a)\leq k$, so $1\leq j_k(a)\leq k$ and
$j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, as required in \Cref{lem:binomial-atom}.
The mean of the binomial variable in \eqref{eq:Bk-derivative} is \(np\).
Its displacement from the atom index satisfies the exact identity
\begin{align}
 2(j-np)
 &=2\left\{j_k(a)-1-(k-1)\frac{1+a}{2}\right\}\notag=k+r_k(a)-2-(k-1)(1+a)\notag\\
 &=r_k(a)-1-(k-1)a\notag\\
 &=k\{h(a)-a\}+(u-1+a).
 \label{eq:derivative-atom-displacement}
\end{align}
The previously proved bounds \(a/2\leq h(a)<a\) imply
\[
 0\leq a-h(a)\leq\frac a2.
\]
Also, \(0<u\leq2\) and, for \(k\geq C^2\),
\(0\leq a\leq C/\sqrt{k}\leq1\), so \(|u-1+a|\leq2\).  Taking absolute
values in \eqref{eq:derivative-atom-displacement} gives
\begin{align*}
 2|j-np|
 &\leq k|h(a)-a|+|u-1+a| \leq\frac{ka}{2}+2 \leq\left(\frac C2+2\right)\sqrt{k}.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 |j-np|
 \leq\left(\frac C4+1\right)\sqrt{k}.
 \label{eq:derivative-atom-near-mean}
\end{equation}

Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial-atom} is stated using \(\sqrt n=\sqrt{k-1}\).
For \(k\geq2\),
\[
 \sqrt{k}\leq\sqrt2\sqrt{k-1}=\sqrt2\sqrt n,
\]
so \eqref{eq:derivative-atom-near-mean} implies
\[
 |j-np|\leq A\sqrt n,
 \qquad
 A:=\sqrt2\left(\frac C4+1\right)=\frac{7\sqrt2}{4}.
\]
In addition, for all sufficiently large \(k\),
\(a\leq C/\sqrt{k}\leq1/3\), and hence
\[
 p=\frac{1+a}{2}\in[1/2,2/3]\subseteq[1/3,2/3].
\]
For this value of $A$, the proof of \Cref{lem:binomial-atom} permits
the choices
\[
 n_A=882,
 \qquad
 c_A=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}
      \exp\left\{-\frac23-\frac83A^2\right\}
     =\sqrt{\frac2\pi}e^{-17},
\]
where the last equality uses $A^2=49/8$.  Thus all hypotheses of that
lemma hold uniformly for $k\geq883$, and
\[
 \mathbb P\left\{
 \operatorname{Bin}\left(k-1,\frac{1+a}{2}\right)=j_k(a)-1
 \right\}
 \geq\frac{c_A}{\sqrt{k-1}}
 \geq\frac{c_A}{\sqrt{k}}.
\]
Substituting this estimate into \eqref{eq:Bk-derivative} gives, with
$\gamma=c_A/2>0$,
\begin{equation}
 B_k'(a)\geq\gamma\sqrt{k}
 \label{eq:Bk-derivative-lower}
\end{equation}
for almost every \(a\in[0,C/\sqrt{k}]\).

Because \(B_k\) is absolutely continuous, the Fundamental Theorem of
Calculus for absolutely continuous functions and
\eqref{eq:Bk-derivative-lower} imply that, for
\(0\leq x<y\leq C/\sqrt{k}\),
\begin{align*}
 B_k(y)-B_k(x)
 &=\int_x^y B_k'(a)\,da\\
 &\geq\gamma\sqrt{k}(y-x)>0.
\end{align*}
Thus \(B_k\) is strictly increasing on \([0,C/\sqrt{k}]\).  Together with
continuity, \(B_k(0)=0\), and \(B_k(C/\sqrt{k})>3/8\), this proves that
the generalised inverse is an ordinary inverse on the relevant range and
that
\[
 B_k(B_k^{-1}(b))=b,
 \qquad 0\leq b\leq3/8.
\]

Finally, let \(0\leq b_0<b_1\leq3/8\) and put
\(\alpha_i=B_k^{-1}(b_i)\).  Both inverse values lie in
\([0,C/\sqrt{k}]\), so the preceding integrated derivative bound gives
\[
 b_1-b_0
 =B_k(\alpha_1)-B_k(\alpha_0)
 \geq\gamma\sqrt{k}(\alpha_1-\alpha_0).
\]
Rearranging and taking
$L=\gamma^{-1}=2/c_A=\sqrt{2\pi}e^{17}$ proves
\eqref{eq:Bk-inverse-lipschitz}.  Since strict increase and \(B_k(0)=0\)
give \(B_k^{-1}(0)=0\), setting \(b_0=0\) proves
\eqref{eq:Bk-inverse-size} and completes the proof.

label: eq:register-worst-average-equality
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a delayed-register kernel and write \(u=jk+s\), where
\(j\in\mathbb Z_+\) and \(0\leq s<k\). If
\(\rho_s(x):=(x_{s+1},\ldots,x_k,x_1,\ldots,x_s)\), then the register
at time \(u\), started from \(x\), has the form
\(\rho_s(x)\odot W_{j,s}\), where \(\odot\) denotes coordinatewise
multiplication and the law of \(W_{j,s}\) does not depend on \(x\).
The map \(z\mapsto\rho_s(x)\odot z\) is a bijection of
\(\{-1,+1\}^k\) preserving \(U_k\). Hence the distance from \(U_k\)
is the same for every initial word, and therefore
\begin{equation}
 \max_x\left\|(P_{k,a}^{\mathrm{dr}})^u(x,\cdot)-U_k\right\|_{\operatorname{TV}}
 =\beta_a(u).
 \label{eq:register-worst-average-equality}
\end{equation}
Before \(k\), \eqref{eq:register-preflush} keeps this common distance
above \(1/2\), so $t_{\mathrm{mix}}\geq k$. At time \(k\), the chain $P_{0}^{\mathrm{dr}}$ crosses $1/4$, since $a_0=B_k^{-1}\{\xi(1-\epsilon)\}$, which by its crossing-time definition \eqref{eq:Bk-inverse}, implies that
\(\beta_{a_0}(k)=\xi(1-\epsilon)\leq1/4\) (since $\xi\leq 1/4$ and $\epsilon>0$). For the other chain, $P_1^{\mathrm{dr}}$,
\(\beta_{a_1}(2k)\leq\xi(1-\epsilon)\leq1/4\). This proves the
claimed worst-case mixing-time bounds.

The worst-case and average mixing times agree at a common
threshold for the delayed register chain, as shown by \eqref{eq:register-worst-average-equality}.
The calculations following
\eqref{eq:register-block-identity} give
\(t_{\mathrm{mix},P_0^{\mathrm{dr}}}^{\sharp}(\xi)=k\) and
\(k<t_{\mathrm{mix},P_1^{\mathrm{dr}}}^{\sharp}(\xi)\leq2k\).
Since \(\xi\leq1/4\), threshold monotonicity and the preceding
worst-case bounds give the result.

title: Proof
body_md: Every entry of \(K_\theta\) is positive. In each checkerboard, the two signed perturbations in a paired row cancel, as do those in a paired column. Thus \(K_\theta\) has every row and column sum equal to one. Inspection of the two block rows and block columns in~\eqref{eq:rr-kernel} then shows that \(P_\theta\) is doubly stochastic. Its stationary law is therefore uniform. Moreover, one refresh already reaches any state in the opposite region and two refreshes reach any state in the initial region. Since every state also has a positive self-loop, \(P_\theta\) is uniformly ergodic.

title: Proof
body_md:
For a rare-refresh checkerboard kernel \(P=P_\theta\), with
\(\theta\in(-1,1)^{2M}\), write
\(d_\theta(t):=\max_x\|P_\theta^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\operatorname{TV}}\). The row
calculation in Lemma~\ref{lem:common-average-mixing-coefficient} gives
\(b_t\leq d_\theta(t)\leq b_t+w_t/2\). At \(t=R/2\),
\(r_t\geq e^{-50/99}\); at \(t=4R\),
\(r_t\leq e^{-4}\), \(p_t\leq e^{-8}\), and
\(w_t\leq4e^{-3.99}\). Hence the envelope gives
\begin{align*}
    d_\theta(R/2)&\geq\frac{31}{32}e^{-50/99}>\frac14,\\
    d_\theta(4R)&\leq e^{-4}+\frac{e^{-8}}{64}+2e^{-3.99}<\frac14.
\end{align*}

Total-variation contraction proves the worst-case bounds.

The calculation proving \eqref{eq:rr-theorem-target-scale} gives \(2R<t_{\mathrm{mix},P}^{\sharp}(1/20)\leq10R\). Moreover,
\(\beta_P(t)\leq d_{\rm max}(t)\) and the submultiplicative
worst-case bound give
\begin{align*}
    t_{\mathrm{mix},P}^{\sharp}(1/20) &\leq t_{\mathrm{mix},P}(1/20) \leq\left\lceil\log_2(20)\right\rceil t_{\mathrm{mix},P}(1/4)\\
    &=5t_{\mathrm{mix},P}(1/4).
\end{align*}
Combining these inequalities with the worst-case bounds above proves the result.

label: eq:rr-confidence-coefficients
title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:rr-confidence-lag-bounds} gives $0<p<0.0014$, $w>0.117$ and $b\in (0.0344875,0.037)$.
Define the desired threshold levels \(L_0:=\xi_0-\eta\) and
\(L_1:=\xi_0+21\eta/20\), and set
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 c_0&=\frac{4(\xi_0-\eta-b)+p/2}{w},\\
 c_1&=\frac{4(\xi_0+21\eta/20-b)+p/2}{w}.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:rr-confidence-coefficients}
\end{equation}
Since \(\eta=\xi_0\epsilon=\epsilon/20\), and \(\epsilon\leq1/4\),
\[
 L_0=\xi_0(1-\epsilon)\geq0.0375>b.
\]
Equation~\eqref{eq:rr-confidence-coefficients} therefore gives
\(c_0-p/(2w)=4(L_0-b)/w>0\). Therefore, $g_{s_{0,1}}(c_0)>0$. Subtracting the two definitions in
\eqref{eq:rr-confidence-coefficients} gives
\[
 c_1-c_0=\frac{41\eta}{5w}>0,
\]
so $c_1>c_0>0$ also satisfies $g_{s_{0,1}}(c_1)>0$. Also,
\(L_1\leq0.063125\), and~\eqref{eq:rr-confidence-lag-bounds} gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 4(L_1-b)+\frac p2
 &<4(0.063125-0.0344875)+0.0007\\
 &=0.11525<0.99(0.117)<0.99w.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(c_1<0.99\), while \(w>0.117\) gives
\[
 c_1-c_0<\frac{41}{5(0.117)}\eta<71\eta.
\]
Since \(p>0\), we have \(0<c_0<c_1<0.99\), so both coefficients are admissible (i.e. lie in $(-1,1)$, as assumed). Hinge positivity (i.e., $wc_i>p/2$ for $i\in\{0,1\}$) gives
\(g_{s_{0,1}}(c_i)=wc_i-p/2\). Substituting
\eqref{eq:rr-confidence-coefficients} into~\eqref{eq:rr-common-profile} therefore yields~\eqref{eq:rr-confidence-profile-values}. The second value is strictly larger than \(\xi_0+\eta\), so monotonicity of $\beta_{c}(t)$ yields the stated crossing-time ordering and disjoint output sets.

title: Proof

The accuracy condition, the bound $p\geq e^{-320/49}$ from
Lemma~\ref{lem:rr-localised-lag-bounds}, and
$\gamma_\ell\geq a_\star/\ell$ give
$\eta\leq c_{\rm acc}/\ell\leq p\gamma_\ell/128$, and hence
$$
h=32\eta/(w\gamma_\ell)\leq p/(4w)=\tau/2.
$$(Recall that the universal constants $\gamma_\ell,~a_\star$ and $c_{\rm acc}$ are defined in Appendix \ref{app:rr-constants}.) The same lemma gives
$0<\tau<0.00658$. Since $U=\tau+hZ$, $|Z|\leq1$ and $h\leq \tau/2$,
\[
 \frac{\tau}{2}\leq\tau-h\leq U\leq\tau+h
 \leq\frac{3\tau}{2}<\frac{3}{200}.
\]
This proves the claimed support inclusion for both translated priors.

title: Proof
body_md:
Under prior $\mu_i$, the random variables $g_{s_{0,2}}(U_e)$ are independent, $[0,wh]$-valued, and have mean $\bar g_i$. Therefore, the (one-sided) Hoeffding's inequality gives,

\begin{align*}
   \mathbb{P}_{\mu_0^{\otimes M}}(\mathcal{U}_0^c)
   &=
   \mathbb{P}_{\mu_0^{\otimes M}}\left\{
   \frac1M\sum_{e=1}^M g_{s_{0,2}}(U_e)-\bar g_0>8\eta
   \right\}\\
   &\leq
   \exp\left\{-\frac{2M(8\eta)^2}{(wh)^2}\right\},
\end{align*}
and
\begin{align*}
   \mathbb{P}_{\mu_1^{\otimes M}}(\mathcal{U}_1^c) &= \mathbb{P}_{\mu_1^{\otimes M}}\left\{
   \frac1M\sum_{e=1}^M g_{s_{0,2}}(U_e)-\bar g_1\leq-8\eta
   \right\}\\
   &\leq
   \exp\left\{-\frac{2M(8\eta)^2}{(wh)^2}\right\}.
\end{align*}
Then, inserting \eqref{eq:loc-translated-prior}, and recalling the constant bounds in \Cref{asm:2} and \eqref{eq:loc-unit-hinge-gap},  yields \(2M(8\eta)^2/(wh)^2=M\gamma_\ell^2/8\geq\log80\). Hence \(\mathbb{P}_{\mu_i^{\otimes M}}(\mathcal{U}_i^c)\leq1/80\) for both \(i\in\{0,1\}\).

For \(u\in\mathcal U_0\), equations~\eqref{eq:loc-split-profile} and~\eqref{eq:loc-control-calibration} give
\[
 \beta_{(c,u)}(s_{0,2})
 \leq \mathbb E_0\beta_{(c,\boldsymbol U)}(s_{0,2})+\eta
 =\xi_0-\eta=\frac{1-\epsilon}{20}.
\]
Similarly, every \(u\in\mathcal U_1\) satisfies
\[
 \beta_{(c,u)}(s_{0,2})
 >\mathbb E_1\beta_{(c,\boldsymbol U)}(s_{0,2})-\eta
 =\xi_0+\eta=\frac{1+\epsilon}{20}.
\]

$\log\frac1{4\delta}\geq\frac13\log\frac4\delta\quad\forall \quad0<\delta\leq\frac{1}{16}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\log x > 0$ whenever $x>1$, we have
\[
 3\log\frac1{4\delta}-\log\frac4\delta
 =\log\frac{1}{256\delta^2}=2\log\frac1{16\delta}\geq0.

head: environment

label: lem:h-equivalence
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:h-equivalence}
Fix $k\in\mathbb N$.  For $0\leq a<1$, let $P_a$ be the product law of
$k$ Rademacher variables $Z_1,\ldots,Z_k$ of mean $a$, let
$P_0=U_k$, and put
\[
 S=\sum_{i=1}^k Z_i,
 \qquad X=\frac{k+S}{2}.
\]
For $0<a<1$, define
\[
 h(a):=\frac{-\log(1-a^2)}{\log((1+a)/(1-a))},
\]
and set $h(0):=0$.  Then $h$ is continuous and strictly increasing on
$[0,1)$, and
\[
 \frac a2\leq h(a)<a,
 \qquad 0<a<1.
\]
For $0\leq a<1$, let $r_k(a)$ be the smallest point of
$\{-k,-k+2,\ldots,k\}$ strictly larger than $kh(a)$, and put
$j_k(a)=(k+r_k(a))/2$.  For $0<a<1$,
\[
 \left\{\frac{dP_a}{dP_0}>1\right\}
 =\{S>kh(a)\}
 =\{S\geq r_k(a)\}
 =\{X\geq j_k(a)\}.
\]
Moreover, for $0\leq a<1$, with $p=(1+a)/2$,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 B_k(a)
 &=\|P_a-P_0\|_{\operatorname{TV}}\\
 &=\mathbb P\{\operatorname{Bin}(k,p)\geq j_k(a)\}
   -\mathbb P\{\operatorname{Bin}(k,1/2)\geq j_k(a)\}.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:Bk-binomial-tail}
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Binomial upper-tail representation of total variation

title: Proof
body_md:
If a realisation has sum $S$, then it contains $(k+S)/2$ plus signs
and $(k-S)/2$ minus signs.  Independence therefore gives
\[
 \frac{dP_a}{dP_0}
 =(1+a)^{(k+S)/2}(1-a)^{(k-S)/2}.
\]
Taking logarithms and collecting the terms involving $k$ and $S$
yields
\[
 \log\frac{dP_a}{dP_0}
 =\frac{k}{2}\log(1-a^2)
  +\frac S2\log\frac{1+a}{1-a}.
\]

We next derive the integral representation for $h$ used
below.  Direct differentiation gives
\begin{align*}
 \frac{d}{du}\{-\log(1-u^2)\}
 &=-\frac{-2u}{1-u^2}
 =\frac{2u}{1-u^2},\\
 \frac{d}{du}\log\frac{1+u}{1-u}
 &=\frac{d}{du}\{\log(1+u)-\log(1-u)\}\\
 &=\frac1{1+u}+\frac1{1-u}
 =\frac{2}{1-u^2}.
\end{align*}
Both logarithmic expressions vanish at \(u=0\).  The Fundamental Theorem
of Calculus therefore gives
\[
 -\log(1-a^2)=\int_0^a\frac{2u}{1-u^2}\,du,
 \quad
 \log\frac{1+a}{1-a}=\int_0^a\frac{2}{1-u^2}\,du,
\]
and hence
\[
 h(a)=
 \frac{\displaystyle\int_0^a u\,w(u)\,du}
      {\displaystyle\int_0^a w(u)\,du},
 \qquad
 w(u):=\frac{2}{1-u^2}.
\]
Thus \(h(a)\) is the weighted average of \(u\) over \([0,a]\), with
positive increasing weight \(w\).  Since \(u\leq a\) and \(w(u)>0\),
\[
 u w(u)\leq a w(u),
\]
with strict inequality for \(0\leq u<a\).  Therefore
\[
 \int_0^a u w(u)\,du
 <a\int_0^a w(u)\,du.
\]
Dividing by the positive total weight \(\int_0^a w(u)\,du\) proves that
\(h(a)<a\).

We next prove that this weighted average is at least the midpoint \(a/2\).
Since \(\int_0^a w(u)\,du>0\), the desired inequality is equivalent to
\begin{align*}
 h(a)\geq\frac a2
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \int_0^a u w(u)\,du
 \geq\frac a2\int_0^a w(u)\,du\\
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \int_0^a\left(u-\frac a2\right)w(u)\,du\geq0.
\end{align*}
Thus it remains to prove that the last centred integral is nonnegative.
Split it at \(a/2\):
\begin{align*}
 I
 &:=
 \int_0^a\left(u-\frac a2\right)w(u)\,du=
 \int_0^{a/2}\left(u-\frac a2\right)w(u)\,du
 +\int_{a/2}^a\left(u-\frac a2\right)w(u)\,du.
\end{align*}
The first integral is nonpositive and the second is nonnegative.  To compare
their magnitudes, make the change of variables \(v=a-u\) in the second
integral.  Then \(u=a-v\), \(du=-dv\), and the transformed endpoints are
\(v=a/2\) when \(u=a/2\) and \(v=0\) when \(u=a\).  Hence
\begin{align*}
 \int_{a/2}^a\left(u-\frac a2\right)w(u)\,du
 &=
 -\int_{a/2}^{0}\left(\frac a2-v\right)w(a-v)\,dv\\
 &=
 \int_0^{a/2}\left(\frac a2-v\right)w(a-v)\,dv\\
 &=
 \int_0^{a/2}\left(\frac a2-u\right)w(a-u)\,du.
\end{align*}
The second equality uses
\(\int_b^c f(v)\,dv=-\int_c^b f(v)\,dv\): the minus sign from
\(du=-dv\) cancels the minus sign introduced by reversing the endpoints.
The final equality merely renames the dummy variable \(v\) as \(u\).
Since
\[
 \int_0^{a/2}\left(u-\frac a2\right)w(u)\,du
 =
 -\int_0^{a/2}\left(\frac a2-u\right)w(u)\,du,
\]
the two halves combine to give
\begin{align*}
 I
 &=
 \int_0^{a/2}\left(\frac a2-u\right)
       \{w(a-u)-w(u)\}\,du\geq0,
\end{align*}
because \(a-u\geq u\) on \([0,a/2]\) and \(w\) is increasing.  By the
equivalence above, \(I\geq0\) proves \(h(a)\geq a/2\).

Finally, write
\[
 N(a):=\int_0^a u w(u)\,du,
 \qquad
 D(a):=\int_0^a w(u)\,du,
\]
so that \(h(a)=N(a)/D(a)\).  The variable \(a\) appears in these
integrals through their upper endpoints.  The Fundamental Theorem of
Calculus therefore gives
\[
 N'(a)=a w(a),
 \qquad
 D'(a)=w(a).
\]
Since \(D(a)>0\), the quotient rule yields
\begin{align*}
 h'(a)
 &=
 \frac{N'(a)D(a)-N(a)D'(a)}{D(a)^2} =
 \frac{a w(a)D(a)-N(a)w(a)}{D(a)^2}\\
 &=
 \frac{w(a)}{D(a)}
 \left\{a-\frac{N(a)}{D(a)}\right\} =
 \frac{w(a)\{a-h(a)\}}{\int_0^a w(u)\,du}.
\end{align*}
Here \(w(a)>0\), \(D(a)>0\), and the previously proved inequality
\(h(a)<a\) gives \(a-h(a)>0\).  Consequently \(h'(a)>0\) for \(a>0\).
The defining quotient is continuous on $(0,1)$, while the bounds above
give $h(a)\to0=h(0)$ as $a\downarrow0$.  Thus $h$ is continuous on
$[0,1)$.  Together with $h'(a)>0$ for $a>0$ and
$h(a)>0=h(0)$, this proves that $h$ is strictly increasing and that
\[
 \frac a2\leq h(a)<a,
 \qquad 0<a<1.
\]

The definition of \(h\) makes its likelihood-ratio role explicit.  For
\(a>0\), the preceding formula for the log likelihood ratio can be
rewritten as
\[
 \log\frac{dP_a}{dP_0}
 =
 \frac12\log\frac{1+a}{1-a}\{S-kh(a)\}.
\]
Indeed, after multiplying out, the definition
\[
 h(a)=\frac{-\log(1-a^2)}{\log((1+a)/(1-a))}
\]
turns the term involving \(h(a)\) into
\((k/2)\log(1-a^2)\).  The factor outside the braces is positive, so
\[
 \frac{dP_a}{dP_0}>1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S>kh(a).
\]
Since $S$ takes values in the lattice $\{-k,-k+2,\ldots,k\}$, the
definitions of $r_k(a)$, $j_k(a)$, and $X$ give
\[
 \{S>kh(a)\}=\{S\geq r_k(a)\}=\{X\geq j_k(a)\}.
\]
Thus the event on which the likelihood ratio exceeds one is a binomial
upper-tail event, namely $\{X\geq j_k(a)\}$.

For two probability mass functions $p$ and $q$ on a finite set,
\[
 \|p-q\|_{\operatorname{TV}}
 =\sum_{x:p(x)>q(x)}\{p(x)-q(x)\}.
\]
Because $P_0$ has full support, the event on which the likelihood ratio
exceeds one collects exactly the positive terms in the signed mass difference
and realises total variation.  Since the definition of $B_k$ gives
$B_k(a)=\|P_a-P_0\|_{\operatorname{TV}}$, it follows that
\[
 B_k(a)
 =P_a\{S>kh(a)\}-P_0\{S>kh(a)\}.
\]
Under $P_a$, $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(k,(1+a)/2)$, whereas under
$P_0$, $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(k,1/2)$.  The preceding event
equivalences therefore prove~\eqref{eq:Bk-binomial-tail} for $a>0$.
At $a=0$, both binomial upper-tail probabilities are equal and $B_k(0)=0$,
so the identity also holds at that endpoint.
head: environment

label: lem:binomial-equivalent-derivative
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Derivative of $B_k$

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $p=(1+a)/2$, and write $P_p$ and $\mathbb E_p$ for probability and
expectation when $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(k,p)$.  By
\eqref{eq:Bk-binomial-tail}, $B_k(a)$ is the difference of the two
corresponding binomial upper-tail probabilities.

Because \(h\) is strictly increasing, the lattice threshold \(r_k(a)\)
is piecewise constant and changes at only finitely many values of \(a\).
Fix an open interval on which \(r_k(a)\), and hence \(j_k(a)\), has a
constant value \(j\).  On this interval, the second term in
\eqref{eq:Bk-binomial-tail} is constant.  Term-by-term differentiation of
the first, finite binomial sum gives
\begin{align}
 \frac{d}{dp}P_p\{X\geq j\}
 &=\sum_{x=j}^k
   \frac{d}{dp}\left\{\binom{k}{x}p^x(1-p)^{k-x}\right\}\notag \\
   &=\sum_{x=j}^k\binom{k}{x}p^x(1-p)^{k-x}
   \left\{\frac{x}{p}-\frac{k-x}{1-p}\right\}\notag\\
   &=\frac{1}{p(1-p)}
   \mathbb E_p[(X-kp)\mathbf 1\{X\geq j\}].
 \label{eq:binomial-tail-score}
\end{align}
To evaluate the final expectation, the binomial identities
\[
 x\binom{k}{x}=k\binom{k-1}{x-1},
 \qquad
 (k-x)\binom{k}{x}=k\binom{k-1}{x}
\]
give
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E_p[X\mathbf 1\{X\geq j\}]
 &=kp\mathbb P\{\operatorname{Bin}(k-1,p)\geq j-1\},\\
 \mathbb E_p[(k-X)\mathbf 1\{X\geq j\}]
 &=k(1-p)\mathbb P\{\operatorname{Bin}(k-1,p)\geq j\}.
\end{align*}
Since \(X-kp=(1-p)X-p(k-X)\), subtracting the two adjacent tails leaves
one atom:
\[
 \mathbb E_p[(X-kp)\mathbf 1\{X\geq j\}]
 =kp(1-p)\mathbb P\{\operatorname{Bin}(k-1,p)=j-1\}.
\]
Substitution into \eqref{eq:binomial-tail-score} therefore yields
\[
 \frac{d}{dp}P_p\{X\geq j\}
 =k\mathbb P\{\operatorname{Bin}(k-1,p)=j-1\}.
\]
Finally, $dp/da=1/2$.  The chain rule gives
\eqref{eq:Bk-derivative} whenever the lattice threshold is locally
constant.  There are only finitely many exceptional points at which the threshold changes.  Moreover, from its
definition as total variation, \(B_k\) is a finite sum of absolute values
of analytic functions of $a$.  It is therefore continuous and locally
absolutely continuous on $[0,1)$.  Thus \eqref{eq:Bk-derivative} holds
almost everywhere.
head: environment

label: lem:binomial-atom
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:binomial-atom}
For every finite \(A>0\), there exist constants \(c_A>0\) and
\(n_A\in\mathbb N\) such that, whenever \(n\geq n_A\),
\(p\in[1/3,2/3]\), and \(j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) satisfy
\(|j-np|\leq A\sqrt n\),
\[
 \mathbb P\{\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)=j\}
 \geq\frac{c_A}{\sqrt n}.
\]
head: environment
name: Finite binomial atom bound

title: Proof
body_md:
Put \(q=j/n\).  The assumption
\(|j-np|\leq A\sqrt n\) implies that
\[
 |q-p|\leq\frac{A}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Choose
\[
 n_A=\left\lceil\max\{4,144A^2\}\right\rceil.
\]
If \(n\geq n_A\), then
\[
 |q-p|\leq\frac{A}{\sqrt n}\leq\frac1{12}.
\]
Since \(p\in[1/3,2/3]\), it follows that \(q\in[1/4,3/4]\).
Thus \(j\) and \(n-j\) are both positive and of order \(n\), and the
Stirling and Taylor bounds below hold uniformly.  In particular,
\(j,n-j\geq n/4\geq1\), so Robbins' formula applies to all three
factorials in \(n!/[j!(n-j)!]\) = $\binom{n}{j}$.

For every positive integer \(m\), write Robbins' formula as
\[
 m!=\sqrt{2\pi m}\left(\frac me\right)^m e^{r_m},
 \qquad
 \frac1{12m+1}<r_m<\frac1{12m}.
\]
Substitution into the binomial coefficient gives
\begin{align*}
 \binom nj
 &=
 \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
 \sqrt{\frac{n}{j(n-j)}}
 \frac{n^n}{j^j(n-j)^{n-j}}
 \exp\{r_n-r_j-r_{n-j}\}.
\end{align*}
Here the factors involving \(e\) cancel because
\[
 e^{-n}e^je^{n-j}=1,
\]
while the three Robbins correction factors collect into
\(\exp\{r_n-r_j-r_{n-j}\}\).  For the square-root factor, the identities
\(j=qn\) and \(n-j=(1-q)n\) give
\[
 \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sqrt{\frac{n}{j(n-j)}}
 =
 \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi n q(1-q)}}.
\]
For the power factor, taking logarithms and making the same substitution
shows how the binary entropy arises:
\begin{align*}
 \log\left(\frac{n^n}{j^j(n-j)^{n-j}}\right)
 &=n\log n-j\log j-(n-j)\log(n-j)\\
 &=n\log n-qn\log(qn)-(1-q)n\log((1-q)n)\\
 &=n\log n-qn\{\log q+\log n\} -(1-q)n\{\log(1-q)+\log n\}\\
 &=-qn\log q-(1-q)n\log(1-q)\\
 &=nH(q),
\end{align*}
where \(H(q):=-q\log q-(1-q)\log(1-q)\).  Exponentiating therefore gives
\[
 \frac{n^n}{j^j(n-j)^{n-j}}=\exp\{nH(q)\}.
\]
Combining the square-root, power, and remainder factors yields
\[
 \binom nj
 =
 \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi n q(1-q)}}
 \exp\{nH(q)\}
 \exp\{r_n-r_j-r_{n-j}\}.
\]
Since \(q\in[1/4,3/4]\),
\[
 j=nq\geq\frac n4,
 \qquad
 n-j=n(1-q)\geq\frac n4.
\]
Moreover, \(r_n>0\), while the upper bound in Robbins' formula gives
\[
 r_j<\frac1{12j},
 \qquad
 r_{n-j}<\frac1{12(n-j)}.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 r_n-r_j-r_{n-j}
 &>-\frac1{12j}-\frac1{12(n-j)}\geq-\frac1{3n}-\frac1{3n}=-\frac{2}{3n}\geq-\frac23.
\end{align*}
Also \(q(1-q)\leq1/4\), and hence
\begin{align*}
 \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi n q(1-q)}}
 &\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi n(1/4)}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi n}}.
\end{align*}
Multiplying the preceding formula for \(\binom nj\) by
\(p^j(1-p)^{n-j}\), and using the exact identity
\begin{align*}
 H(q)+q\log p+(1-q)\log(1-p)
 &=-q\log\frac qp-(1-q)\log\frac{1-q}{1-p}=-\operatorname{kl}(q\Vert p),
\end{align*}
where \(\operatorname{kl}(q\Vert p)\) is the one-trial Bernoulli
relative entropy, therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb P\{\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)=j\}
 \geq\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\,\frac1{\sqrt n}
       \exp\left\{-\frac23-n\operatorname{kl}(q\Vert p)\right\}.
\]

For fixed \(p\), let \(f_p(x)=\operatorname{kl}(x\Vert p)\).  Then for all $x\in[1/4,3/4]$,
\[
 f_p(p)=f_p'(p)=0,
 \qquad
 f_p''(x)=\frac1{x(1-x)}\leq\frac{16}{3}.
\]
The segment between \(p\) and \(q\) lies in this interval, so Taylor's
theorem gives
\[
 \operatorname{kl}(q\Vert p)
 \leq\frac83(q-p)^2.
\]
Consequently \(n\operatorname{kl}(q\Vert p)\leq8A^2/3\), and the claimed
bound follows, for instance, with
\[
 c_A=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}
      \exp\left\{-\frac23-\frac83A^2\right\}.
\]

label: lem:rr-confidence-lag-bounds
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For \(0<x<1\), the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives
\[
 \log(1-x)=-\int_0^x\frac{du}{1-u},
\]
and bounding the integrand on \([0,x]\) yields
\[
 -\frac{x}{1-x}\leq\log(1-x)\leq-x.
\]
Applying these bounds with \(x=1/R\), and using
\(R/(R-1)\leq100/99\), gives
\[
 e^{-10/3}\leq r=(1-1/R)^{33R/10}\leq e^{-3.3}.
\]
Since \(e^{-10/3}>0.0356\) and \(e^{-3.3}<0.037\), this proves the
stated bounds on \(r\). Applying the upper logarithmic bound with
\(x=2/R\) gives
\[
 0<p=(1-2/R)^{33R/10}\leq e^{-6.6}<0.0014.
\]
From the definition of \(w\),
\[
 w=\frac{33}{10}\frac{r}{1-1/R}.
\]
The bounds on \(r\) and \(1-1/R\geq0.99\) give
\(0.117<w<0.124\). Finally, \(p/2<r\), because
\(0<1-2/R<1-1/R\), and
\(1-2/D\geq31/32\) imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 b&=r\left(1-\frac2D\right)+\frac pD<r<0.037,\\
 b&>0.0356\frac{31}{32}=0.0344875.
 \end{aligned}
\]
head: environment

label: lem:rr-localised-lag-bounds
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply the logarithmic inequalities used in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:rr-confidence-lag-bounds}, now at $s_{0,2}=16R/5$,
using $R/(R-1)\leq100/99$ and $R/(R-2)\leq50/49$. This gives the
displayed bounds on $r$ and $p$. The remaining bounds follow from
\[
 w=\frac{16}{5}(1-1/R)^{16R/5-1},\qquad
 \tau=\frac{p}{2w},\qquad
 b=r\left(1-\frac2D\right)+\frac pD,
\]
using $R\geq100$ and $D\geq64$.
